description:
We are Emiliano and Tomi, a team from Buenos Aires, Argentina, passionate about technology, artificial intelligence, software development, and scientific innovation.

Our mission: Turning space data into knowledge for a changing Earth.
summary:
TerraMind Evidence is an interactive environmental research tool that helps people distinguish apparent changes from statistically supported trends.

Our pilot examines a fixed location in Argentina’s Gran Chaco (25° S, 63° W) using 253 real NASA MODIS vegetation composites and 4,018 daily NASA POWER/GPM IMERG precipitation estimates covering 2015–2025.

Through an accessible, Spanish-language interface, users can explore NDVI, EVI and precipitation time series, inspect observation quality, compare seasonal anomalies, change analysis periods, and evaluate trends using Sen’s slope and exploratory Mann–Kendall tests.

Unlike dashboards that only display environmental indicators, TerraMind emphasizes scientific transparency: users can examine quality exclusions, methodological assumptions, data provenance, and downloadable evidence.

Our initial results do not establish statistically significant monotonic trends under the implemented assumptions. Rather than hiding this uncertainty, TerraMind makes it part of the experience.

The project addresses NASA’s challenge by making environmental trend analysis understandable, traceable, and reproducible, starting with a carefully bounded single-site case study.
details:
The Problem

Satellite observations provide valuable information about environmental change, but interpreting these observations requires more than plotting a line on a chart. Data quality, seasonal variability, missing values, spatial resolution, time-window selection, and statistical assumptions can all influence the conclusions.

TerraMind Evidence addresses this problem by making the reasoning behind environmental trend analysis visible and reproducible.

Our Solution

We developed an interactive, browser-based environmental evidence explorer focused on a pilot location in Argentina's Gran Chaco, at latitude −25° and longitude −63°.

The application analyzes two categories of NASA observations collected between 2015 and 2025:

  • Vegetation: 253 MODIS/Terra MOD13Q1 16-day composites containing NDVI and EVI indicators, at approximately 250 m nominal spatial resolution.
  • Precipitation: 4,018 daily estimates from GPM IMERG, accessed through NASA POWER, with a nominal spatial resolution of 0.1°.

The application provides interactive time-series visualizations, annual summaries, seasonal anomalies, observation-quality filters, selectable analysis periods, and predefined sensitivity comparisons.

Users can review the original observations, inspect exclusions, explore Sen's slope estimates, and examine exploratory Mann–Kendall statistical tests.

An interactive map based on NASA GIBS provides geographic context. Scientific documentation explains the limitations of the observations and the methodology.

Results and supporting evidence can be exported as CSV, SVG, and Markdown files.

Scientific Findings

In the 2015–2025 pilot, the strict-quality NDVI analysis used 238 accepted composites and produced a Sen slope of approximately −0.01152 index units per year, with an exploratory p-value of 0.276.

The corresponding EVI analysis produced a slope of approximately +0.00174 per year and a p-value of 0.640.

The annual IMERG precipitation analysis produced a slope of approximately −0.953 mm per year and a p-value of 1.000.

None of these results supports a statistically significant monotonic trend at the 0.05 threshold under the implemented exploratory tests.

These findings do not demonstrate environmental stability or establish causes. They illustrate why uncertainty must be communicated rather than concealed.

Technology and Implementation

The application was built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js, and Python.

Leaflet supports interactive mapping, while NASA GIBS supplies the geographical imagery. Python scripts retrieve, validate, archive, and reconstruct the NASA datasets.

Original source responses and SHA-256 checksums are preserved to support independent verification. The statistical calculations were cross-checked using an independent Python implementation.

The project documentation records data sources, quality rules, temporal aggregation, analysis assumptions, and known limitations.

OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, testing, interface design, and documentation. The environmental observations themselves were retrieved from NASA services and were not generated by AI.

Creativity and Innovation

TerraMind does not claim to invent a new satellite sensor or statistical algorithm.

Its innovation lies in an evidence-centered user experience: instead of merely displaying an environmental trend, the interface allows users to inspect how that conclusion was obtained, how filtering decisions affect it, and whether the available evidence supports it.

The system is designed to communicate uncertainty as an essential scientific result.

Intended Impact

TerraMind aims to make environmental evidence more understandable for students, researchers, educators, environmental organizations, and other users who need to interpret changes in Earth systems.

The current implementation is a reproducible single-site research pilot. It does not provide regional forest assessments, validated ecological recovery measurements, real-time fire warnings, or operational forecasts.

Future development could extend the approach to multiple locations and additional Earth-observation variables, subject to appropriate scientific validation.
